blindComparison: A stranger picks the Ghost of Tsushima frame, and the reason is not detail density — it is that our image has no colour above the horizon line and no readable organic form in its mid-ground. Recalled from memory, not measured against fetched footage: a Tsushima golden-hour approach puts its most saturated colour in the sky and in the blossom mass, and its treeline reads as individual crowns with trunks and light passing between them. Ours inverts that. In `hero` the sunward sky measures RGB [162.2,165.0,163.4] at saturation 0.03 — literally achromatic — while the ground props carry saturation 0.38-0.45, so the picture reads as warm props composited onto an overcast grey plate. And the two largest organic masses in the set both fail as material: the sakura canopy is a mosaic of hard-edged flat quads in two disjoint hue populations (salmon [174.5,118.9,117.1] against violet [127.0,81.3,98.3], nothing between them), and the mid-ground forest band measures [98.4,98.3,88.5] with R equal to G to 0.1 code values — an olive-grey noise field with no trunk, no crown and no silhouette. Where the build genuinely competes is the near foreground: the backlit wet flagstone in `sun` and `valley` (specular sheet, tight contact shadows, rim-lit susuki) would survive the comparison on its own. The frame loses in the two zones a landscape shot is mostly made of — the sky and the middle distance.
notesForRig: No character or enemy appears in any of the five framings, so E07-CHARACTER (BM-CHAR-01 silhouette, BM-CHAR-02 rim separation) could not be judged from this set at all and is neither passed nor failed here. E09-UI is likewise unjudged: the HUD is blanked by design, which is the capture, not a defect. Nothing below re-files a disproved item: cast shadows are present and correctly long, the vermilion measures correct, the sun disc is in frame at UV ~(0.605,0.455), no floating trees were found, and the god-ray finding below is written as a spread problem, not a gain problem.

findings.problem: The sakura canopy — the single largest colour accent in the hero framing, occupying roughly UV x 0.12-0.34, y 0.10-0.35 — is a mosaic of large flat quads with hard straight cut boundaries and no soft alpha falloff. At native resolution in a 228x140 crop taken at UV (0.20,0.14) every 'blossom cluster' is an angular polygon of one uniform colour meeting its neighbour along a knife edge; there is no petal-scale structure inside any card, no light transmitting through the mass, and no branch structure reading through it. Small hard black wedges (backfacing or self-shadow-acned cards) are scattered through the interior. The colour splits into two disjoint populations with nothing between them: sunlit clusters measure mean RGB [174.5,118.9,117.1] at UV (0.28,0.13,0.04,0.05) — G and B within 2 code values of each other, so the hue is a flat red-orange with no rose lean at all — and shaded clusters measure [127.0,81.3,98.3] at UV (0.17,0.20,0.04,0.05), where B exceeds G by 17, a cold violet. That is roughly a 40-degree hue discontinuity inside one tree with no transition band. In `torii` the same canopy at UV (0.30,0.48,0.06,0.08) is almost entirely the dull violet population and reads as grey-purple mould rather than blossom.
findings.why: At the reference bar, a blossom mass is the softest, most light-permeable object in a golden-hour frame — its whole job is to scatter and glow. Ours reads as torn construction paper pasted over the mountain: the hard card edges destroy the silhouette at every scale, and the two-population hue split makes the tree look like two different materials welded together. This is the first thing a stranger's eye lands on in the hero framing and it is the thing that immediately says 'not shipped'.
findings.fix: Break up the card silhouette and close the hue gap. Targets an owner can verify by re-measuring the same three boxes: (a) the boundary between adjacent blossom cards must stop being a straight line — no card edge longer than ~12 px should be straight at 2532-wide native in the hero framing; (b) the lit and shaded populations must be joined by a measurable transition — sample a 4x4 grid of 0.02x0.02 boxes across UV (0.12-0.34, 0.10-0.35) and require the hue histogram to be unimodal rather than the current two clusters at red-orange and violet; (c) the lit population must read as blossom, not as orange: at UV (0.28,0.13,0.04,0.05) B should sit below G by at least 8 code values (currently B=117.1 vs G=118.9, i.e. -1.8) so the mass reads rose rather than salmon; (d) the shaded population must not lose saturation — currently 0.359, it should hold within 0.05 of the lit side's 0.38 rather than going grey; (e) eliminate the hard black interior wedges — no pixel inside the canopy bounding box should sit below luma 30 unless it is a branch.
findings.hypothesis: The two hue populations look like a front-face/back-face split rather than a lighting gradient, i.e. the cards may be single-sided with an unlit or wrongly-tinted reverse. Disprove this before acting: render the canopy with a constant white albedo and see whether the two-population split survives. If it does, it is geometry/normals, not the blossom tint. Do not act on this guess without that test.

findings.problem: The mid-ground forest / bamboo band — which spans the entire width of the `wide` framing between the plateau and the mountains, roughly UV y 0.36-0.52, and reappears as the whole backdrop of `torii` and `valley` — resolves at native resolution into formless noise. A 253x164 native crop at UV (0.12,0.36) shows vertically-smeared green-on-brown mottle with no readable tree: no trunk, no crown boundary, no gap between individuals, no light-side/shade-side on any single plant. Every element is the same height and the same value, so the band reads as a stamped texture rather than as a mass of objects. It measures mean RGB [98.4,98.3,88.5] at saturation 0.132 — R and G are equal to within 0.1 code values, so the 'forest' is not green, it is olive-grey. For scale of the failure, in the same frame the flagstone measures saturation 0.373-0.477 and the valley ground in `valley` measures 0.628. The band that should be the most alive surface in the picture is the second-least saturated thing in it, after the sky.
findings.why: The mid-ground is the depth plane a landscape composition is built on; BM-WORLD-01 requires three separable planes and this one is present but empty. At the reference bar the treeline at 200-600 m still resolves individual crowns with warm sun-struck tops and cool shaded flanks, and that variation is what sells the distance. A uniform olive band reads as a painted flat, which collapses the picture back to two planes: foreground props and backdrop. It is the difference between a landscape and a diorama.
findings.fix: Give the band individual form and colour separation. Verifiable targets, all measured on the box UV (0.12,0.36,0.10,0.14) in `phone-wide`: (a) saturation must rise from 0.132 to at least 0.30 — it must read as vegetation, not as olive-grey; (b) G must exceed R by at least 12 code values (currently G-R = -0.1); (c) individual plants must become separable — the band's lumaSpread is currently 51.2 across the crop; a real treeline at this distance separates sun-struck crown from shaded flank and should reach at least 90 there, with the brightest crowns carrying the warm key (R-B >= 25) and the flanks carrying the cool fill (B-R >= 0); (d) height variation must be visible in silhouette against the mountain — the top edge of the band should vary by at least +/-15% of mean plant height rather than reading as a flat cut. Do not solve this by adding more instances; the band is already dense and the failure is that nothing in it is individually readable.
findings.hypothesis: The uniform height and the absence of any trunk suggest the far band may be a different, cheaper representation than the near bamboo in `valley` (which does resolve individual culms and leaves correctly at UV 0.02-0.10). If so the fix belongs at the LOD/impostor transition rather than in the near foliage. Confirm by finding the distance at which culms stop resolving before changing anything.

findings.problem: The sky is achromatic and structureless at what is supposed to be golden hour, and it occupies the top ~35% of the hero framing. Measured on pure-sky patches with no geometry in them: UV (0.88,0.03,0.10,0.12) gives mean RGB [162.2,165.0,163.4] at saturation 0.030 — R, G and B within 3 code values, i.e. neutral grey — and this is the sunward side of the frame. UV (0.88,0.28,0.10,0.08), just above the horizon, gives [178.2,180.0,172.9] at saturation 0.051. Only the far left of the sky carries any hue at all, [148.4,172.8,179.2] at saturation 0.172. Structurally it is empty: a 557x257 native crop at UV (0.30,0.02) contains not one cloud, not one band, not one wisp — detail 0.46-0.55 and lumaSpread 13.9-20.1 across the whole patch. `torii` is the same picture, [114.4,133.8,146.5] at saturation 0.219 with detail 1.01 and no cloud form. The result is a large, bright, flat, colourless field sitting above a warmly lit set.
findings.why: This is the single largest contiguous area in three of the five framings and it is doing nothing. At the reference bar the low-sun sky is the picture: a warm amber-to-rose wash near the horizon deepening to cyan at zenith, with banded cloud catching underlight. A grey sky with no gradient and no cloud reads as overcast midday, which directly contradicts the 13-degree key light and the amber cast on every lit surface below it. The eye registers the time-of-day contradiction before it notices anything else, and it is why the frame reads flat before any object in it is judged.
findings.fix: Put colour and structure back into the sky. Verifiable targets, measured on the same boxes: (a) sunward sky at UV (0.88,0.03,0.10,0.12) must reach saturation >= 0.20 with R exceeding B by at least 25 code values — currently saturation 0.030 and R-B = -1.2, i.e. very slightly cool on the sun side; (b) the near-horizon band at UV (0.88,0.28,0.10,0.08) must be warmer still than the zenith, R-B >= 35 — currently 5.3; (c) a zenith-to-horizon hue gradient must exist across the frame: the anti-sun sky at UV (0.38,0.01) is currently [148.4,172.8,179.2] and the sunward sky [162.2,165.0,163.4], a 20-code hue swing across 1300 px; that swing should be at least 60 code values of R-B between the two sides; (d) cloud structure must exist — a 0.10x0.12 pure-sky patch anywhere in `hero` should measure lumaSpread >= 45 (currently 13.9) with detail >= 2.0 (currently 0.55). Cloud must be soft banding at low sun, not high-frequency noise; the detail figure alone must not be satisfied by grain.
findings.hypothesis: The sunward sky measuring flatly neutral while everything it lights is amber looks like the sky's own colour is being computed independently of the sun's colour, or is being flattened after the fact. Do not act on that as fact — ablate by pushing the sun azimuth 90 degrees and re-measuring UV (0.88,0.03): if the neutral patch stays neutral in the new sunward direction, the sky gradient is not tracking the sun at all, and that is a different fix from a saturation deficit.

findings.problem: The distant terrain — both the valley floor and the mountain range — is desaturated to near-neutral, so the 1.8 km landscape has no colour in it. The open ground at UV (0.08,0.62,0.18,0.10) measures mean RGB [46.0,46.1,46.3]: R, G and B agree to within 0.3 code values, which is exactly grey. A second box at UV (0.55,0.60,0.18,0.06) gives [61.2,61.3,64.0], also grey. The mountain body measures [136.9,125.6,120.1] at saturation 0.119 in `wide` at UV (0.10,0.12,0.08,0.05) and [138.3,128.5,122.9] at saturation 0.105 in `torii` at UV (0.06,0.42,0.12,0.06). Even the snowcaps, which at a 13-degree sun should carry the most saturated colour anywhere in the picture, measure only [211.5,195.0,174.2] at saturation 0.182 — a mild cream, not alpenglow. Whole-frame saturation for `wide` is 0.178, the lowest of the five shots. The visible consequence is that `wide` reads as a greyscale landscape with a small red-and-gold plateau sitting on top of it. The ground surface is also bare: a native crop at UV (0.10,0.72) shows dark mud with sparse tiny black tufts and no readable ground cover at any scale.
findings.why: BM-WORLD-04 asks the terrain to read as mountain rather than as a modelled hill, and this is the reason it does not. Aerial perspective is supposed to shift distance toward the *sky's* hue, not toward neutral — neutral-grey distance is the signature of haze with no colour of its own, and it flattens the whole vista into a value study. Meanwhile the reference's defining landscape image is a wind-driven field with colour in it; an achromatic dirt plane with dots on it cannot carry that, and it is the largest single surface in the frame.
findings.fix: Get colour into the distance. Verifiable targets on the same boxes in `phone-wide`: (a) the open ground at UV (0.08,0.62,0.18,0.10) must move off neutral — currently max channel spread is 0.3 code values; require at least 12 code values of channel spread, with the sunward ground warm (R-B >= 12) and the shaded ground cool (B-R >= 6), so the field carries the same warm/cool split the foreground props already do; (b) the mountain body at UV (0.10,0.12,0.08,0.05) must reach saturation >= 0.20 from 0.119; (c) the snowcap at UV (0.30,0.03,0.08,0.05) must carry alpenglow — R-B >= 55 from the current 37.3 — since it is the highest, most directly sun-struck surface in the frame; (d) the ground must gain readable surface variation: lumaSpread across UV (0.08,0.62,0.18,0.10) is currently 47.7 and should reach at least 80 with visible large-scale patchiness (worn ground, exposed rock, differing cover) rather than uniform mud. Do not fix (a) by raising global saturation — the foreground already measures 0.37-0.63 and would go garish.
findings.hypothesis: Neutral-grey distance where the sky is also neutral is consistent with the distance fade blending toward a fixed grey rather than toward the sky's own colour — but the sky is currently near-neutral too (finding above), so these may be one defect seen twice. Fix the sky first and re-measure the mountain before changing any terrain colour; if the mountain's saturation rises on its own, this finding is already closed and no terrain change is warranted.

findings.problem: The shrine plaza carries no evidence of use. Across the whole flagstone expanse in `torii` — UV roughly (0.15-1.0, 0.60-1.0), the bottom 40% of the frame — there is not one fallen leaf, not one weed in a joint, not one moss patch, not one chip or spall on a stone edge, not one puddle, not one scuff, not one piece of dropped debris, not one worn path where feet actually go. Every joint is clean and every stone is the same grey-brown; the region measures [50.8,38.3,37.1] with no stone-to-stone albedo variation visible at native resolution. The dressing is equally uniform: in `wide` at UV (0.10-0.55, 0.55-0.95) the stone lanterns along the approach are all the same model at the same height, all upright, all with an identical elliptical pool of light at their base, and the sake barrels at UV (0.13,0.85) are a tidy identical stack. Nothing leans, nothing has toppled, nothing has accumulated at its base.
findings.why: R9-DRESSING-001 and BM-WORLD-02 have been open since round 13 and this is what they are pointing at. The compact-courtyard bar (SEKIRO's Ashina courtyards) is met by accumulation: moss in every joint, leaves drifted against walls, a visibly worn line through the middle of the flagstone. Without it a place that is supposed to be old and visited reads as a level editor with props dropped on a clean plane, and the eye reads 'unfinished' even though every individual asset here is competent. The stone lanterns themselves are among the best objects in the set — the failure is that there are twelve identical ones.
findings.fix: Dress the plaza against R9-DRESSING-001 as written, and make the result measurable: (a) spacing between adjacent approach lanterns in `wide` must vary by >= +/-25% of mean spacing and height by >= +/-15%; (b) at least 1 in 4 dressing props must carry a visible lean, weathering difference, or accumulation at its base — currently 0 of the visible set does; (c) the walked path must separate from the off-path plaza by >= 25% in luma, measurable as two boxes of the same size on and off the path in `torii`; (d) add joint-scale accumulation — moss, leaf litter, grit — such that a 0.10x0.10 box anywhere in the plaza in `torii` shows at least three distinct albedo populations rather than the current one. Concentrate accumulation where it would physically collect: against the torii post bases, in the lee of the buildings, and in the low joints.

findings.problem: The two backlit framings deliver a flat milky veil over the mid-field instead of separated light shafts. In `sun`, the box UV (0.10,0.30,0.25,0.25) measures mean [149.8,148.4,141.0] at saturation 0.105 with p50 luma 192.6 — a bright, nearly colourless wash over what should be the most colour-saturated region in the set, sitting directly downsun of the torii. In `valley` the equivalent region UV (0.20,0.15,0.35,0.30) measures [200.1,166.8,116.1] with lumaSpread 118.5 and no shaft structure visible at native resolution: the bamboo edge at UV 0.30-0.55 is silhouetted against the sun and is exactly the occluder that should be cutting the light into discrete beams, and instead the light between the culms and the light behind them is the same undifferentiated brightness. There is no beam anywhere in either frame that a viewer could point at.
findings.why: The backlit-through-bamboo shot is the single image in this set that most directly invokes the reference, and shafts are the whole reason to take it. A uniform veil does the opposite of what shafts do: it lowers local contrast everywhere instead of raising it in a few places, so the mid-field loses its material read (see the achromatic measurements above) while gaining nothing dramatic. It is the reason `sun` looks hazy rather than radiant.
findings.fix: This is a spread problem, not a gain problem — the standing disproof records that raising the gain was already tried and measured as a regression, and that the pass currently smears a ~10%-coverage emitter across 99.9% of the frame. Any change here must reduce the spatial extent of the contribution, not increase its amplitude. Verifiable targets: (a) in `valley`, the ratio between the brightest and dimmest 0.02x0.02 boxes sampled along a horizontal line at UV y=0.30 across x 0.25-0.60 (i.e. across the backlit bamboo edge) must reach at least 2.5:1; it is currently near 1 because the veil is common-mode; (b) the wash floor must come down — the `sun` box UV (0.10,0.30,0.25,0.25) currently sits at p50 luma 192.6 and should drop below 165 while the frame's p99.9 stays above 235 so the sun itself is not dimmed; (c) mid-field saturation in that same `sun` box must rise from 0.105 to at least 0.22 once the veil stops washing it out. If (c) improves as a side effect of (b), that alone closes this finding.

findings.problem: Two large hanging cloth banners sit directly between the camera and a 13-degree sun — at UV roughly (0.335-0.360, 0.55-0.70) and (0.398-0.424, 0.55-0.70) — and both render as opaque matte slabs. Nothing transmits through them, there is no weave, no crease, no fray at the hem, no printed device, and no wind deformation; each is a smooth vertical gradient inside a hard rectangular outline. Measured detail (mean |Laplacian|) is 3.09 on the banner at UV (0.398,0.56,0.026,0.12) against 7.34 on the flagstone beside it at UV (0.40,0.80,0.06,0.08) and 6.30 on the stone lantern post at UV (0.295,0.70,0.020,0.06) — the cloth carries less than half the fine-scale structure of the stone around it, which is backwards for the material.
findings.why: E11's stated principle is grain at every scale with no untextured flat surface anywhere in frame, and these are the flattest surfaces in the set. Worse, they are backlit: thin cloth in front of a low sun is one of the most recognisable images in this genre precisely because it glows and shows its weave. Rendering it as an opaque board throws away the strongest lighting event available in the framing and makes the prop read as a placeholder next to stone and wood that are genuinely well made.
findings.fix: Make the banner behave as thin cloth. Verifiable targets on the box UV (0.398,0.56,0.026,0.12) in `phone-sun`: (a) detail must rise from 3.09 to at least 6.0, matching the stone beside it, via weave and crease structure rather than added noise; (b) the cloth must transmit — with the sun behind it the banner's luma should sit above the same cloth's luma in a non-backlit framing, and its saturation should rise (currently 0.592 with the mean pulled by the surround; the banner interior itself is near-neutral dark); (c) the outline must stop being a clean rectangle — add hem fray and a wind-driven curl so the silhouette varies along its length; (d) carry a printed device so the banner reads as a shrine nobori rather than a blank sheet.

findings.problem: The sun disc is achromatic and small. At UV (0.595,0.42,0.03,0.06) it measures mean RGB [247.7,247.2,238.9] at saturation 0.036 with p50 luma 251.4 — a clean white circle roughly 60 px across in a 2532 px frame — while every surface it lights in the same frame is washed amber. It presents as a hard-edged disc with a tight halo rather than as an atmospheric bloom.
findings.why: It is an internal contradiction the eye catches immediately: a white light source casting orange light. At a 13-degree elevation the disc has passed through enough airmass that it should be the most saturated warm object in the picture, and it should be visibly larger and softer-edged than a clean circle. As drawn it reads as a lens element composited over the scene rather than as the sun in it.
findings.fix: Redden and soften the disc to match the light it is casting. Targets on the same box UV (0.595,0.42,0.03,0.06): (a) saturation from 0.036 to >= 0.25 with R exceeding B by at least 40 code values; (b) the disc edge must soften — lumaSpread across that box is currently 21.9 against a p50 of 251.4, i.e. a near-binary edge; the falloff should span at least 25 px; (c) the apparent diameter should grow to roughly 1.5-2x the current ~60 px so it reads as a low sun rather than a point. Do not solve this by increasing bloom radius globally — the existing bloom around the paper lanterns is already at the edge of reading as a glow filter.
